subject: Computer Networking
title: How Data Travels Through Cables
description: A short lesson to help you apply How Data Travels Through Cables.

hook.text: Your message crosses an ocean in milliseconds. It travels as light through glass thinner than a hair.

buildup.text: Fiber optic cables use pulses of light to carry data. Copper cables use electrical signals instead.

discovery.text: Light in fiber is faster and carries more data. That's why the internet's backbone is fiber, not copper.

twist.text: Undersea cables carry 99% of intercontinental traffic. Satellites handle only a tiny fraction.

climax.text: A single modern undersea cable can carry hundreds of terabits per second across the Atlantic.

punchline.text: The internet's real highway is glass under the ocean.

quiz.question: How does most intercontinental internet traffic travel?

details.summary: Internet data travels as electrical signals through copper cables, light pulses through fiber optic cables, and radio waves through wireless connections. Undersea fiber cables carry over 95 percent of intercontinental traffic. The physical layer determines the speed and capacity of every connection.
details.whyItMatters: The internet feels wireless and abstract but depends on physical infrastructure. Cables determine the speed limits and reliability of global connectivity.
takeaways: Copper carries electrical signals for short distances
Fiber optic uses light pulses for high-speed, long-distance links
Over 95% of intercontinental data travels through undersea cables

faq.question: Why is fiber optic faster than copper?
faq.answer: Light in fiber travels faster and with less signal degradation than electricity in copper. Fiber supports much higher bandwidth because light wavelengths can be multiplexed. Fiber is also immune to electromagnetic interference that degrades copper signals.

faq.question: What happens if an undersea cable breaks?
faq.answer: Traffic reroutes through other cables, but bandwidth drops and latency increases. Specialized cable repair ships locate the break and splice the cable on the ocean floor. Repairs can take weeks. Redundant cable routes provide resilience for critical connections.
